recent_posts.title: "Indie" never really meant "Independent"
recent_posts.summary: An exploration of what 'indie' actually means across industries, tracing the word's origins to a 1927 Variety article about independent Chicago theaters being squeezed by corporate chains. The piece traces indie through music history (Rough Trade Records, UK punk) and into gaming, arguing that 'indie' has evolved from meaning 'independent' into a genre descriptor tied to low production values. Using Clair Obscur: Expedition 33's sweep of the Game Awards as a jumping-off point, it argues the game is genuinely indie by historical standards (small team, independent publisher, creative freedom, ~$10M budget) but doesn't fit the aesthetic genre people associate with indie. The conclusion calls for the games industry to retire 'best indie game' award categories in favor of more descriptive alternatives, similar to how the Grammys use 'best alternative album' instead.

recent_posts.title: A computer graphics YouTuber's 2025 year in review
recent_posts.summary: A computer graphics YouTuber reflects on their creative output in 2025, covering projects like a compute shader wrapper language, a Perlin noise implementation, a PS1 aesthetics demo, a GPU-driven terrain generator with an accompanying game jam (Dirt Jam), and a cellular automaton game made in Godot. The post discusses the challenges of balancing YouTube sponsorship obligations with creative work, burnout cycles, and a harassment campaign following a video critiquing color banding in Hollow Knight: Silksong. Plans for 2026 include dropping strict sponsorship deadlines, developing tools for the graphics community, and presenting at GDOCon Boston. The second half is a personal game-of-the-year roundup with ratings for titles played throughout 2025.

recent_posts.title: What generative AI actually is and why the terminology matters
recent_posts.summary: A critical breakdown of what 'generative AI' actually means technically, arguing that the term deliberately obscures the reality of how these systems work. Covers the distinction between procedural generation and machine learning, explains how models like MidJourney and ChatGPT require massive datasets obtained through scraping (framed as theft), discusses hallucination and lack of true reasoning, the inability to fully control outputs, the impossibility of genuine creativity, and the significant environmental costs of data centers and GPU manufacturing. Concludes that generative AI primarily serves corporate interests at the expense of artists, consumers, and the environment.

recent_posts.title: The Hand Drawn Graphics Of Silksong
recent_posts.summary: A deep technical breakdown of Hollow Knight Silksong's rendering pipeline, examining five core visual components: depth of field, parallax mapping via perspective camera, particle systems, post-processing effects (bloom, vignette), and hand-painted art. The main focus is diagnosing and solving the game's color banding problem caused by low-resolution glow textures being magnified. The analysis covers why Bayer dithering (used in Team Cherry's post-launch patch) fails to fix the issue, and proposes Interleaved Gradient Noise (IGN) as a one-line shader solution that effectively eliminates banding artifacts at minimal performance cost. Practical demonstrations are shown in Godot and ReShade.

recent_posts.title: Building a customizable cellular automaton game from scratch
recent_posts.summary: A developer documents building a customizable real-time cellular automaton game for a game jam, covering the history of cellular automata from Von Neumann to Conway's Game of Life, then explaining how they extended it with custom neighborhoods, multi-neighborhood systems, and GPU-accelerated simulation. Technical highlights include packing neighborhood data into 64-bit integers for efficient GPU transfer via Vulkan push constants, building a tilemap-based UI for drawing custom kernels, implementing bitwise operations to count active neighbors, and generating procedural color palettes using the OKLab color space. The project, called 'God Machine', was built in Godot and includes original music composed using suspended chords.

recent_posts.title: How live service games and gacha mechanics collapsed the gaming industry
recent_posts.summary: A sweeping critique of the video game industry's decline, tracing how always-on DRM, mobile freemium models (Farmville, Angry Birds), gacha mechanics, and the live service blueprint pioneered by Destiny and Fortnite transformed gaming from complete single-player experiences into perpetual monetization engines. The piece argues that venture capitalist and executive pressure—not consumer demand—drove the shift toward multiplayer-only, gambling-integrated, intentionally incomplete games. It concludes with a detailed breakdown of Uma Musume's gacha economics, showing how a single support card can cost up to $2,100 at worst-case pity, and frames the Stop Killing Games initiative as a rare consumer-rights pushback against these industry trends.

recent_posts.title: Sculpting Terrain With Math
recent_posts.summary: A beginner-friendly walkthrough of procedural terrain generation using math, covering mesh creation, vertex shaders, Perlin noise, and fractional Brownian motion. Starting from a flat plane rendered via GPU draw calls, the tutorial builds up to a customizable terrain system using layered noise with adjustable amplitude, frequency, lacunarity, and domain rotation. The post argues that dropping the 'game-ready' requirement makes terrain generation an excellent learning project for beginner graphics programmers, touching on rendering pipelines, winding order, Lambertian lighting, and slope-based coloring. It concludes with a community jam invitation to extend the terrain generator.

recent_posts.title: Understanding The PS1 Aesthetic
recent_posts.summary: A deep technical breakdown of the PS1 GPU's visual quirks and how to replicate them in a modern game engine (Godot). Covers the hardware constraints behind the iconic PS1 look: low-resolution render targets, affine texture mapping (perspective-incorrect interpolation), integer clip-space vertex snapping, Gouraud vertex lighting, Silent Hill's dual-pass fog technique, 15-bit color quantization, and the PS1's proprietary 4x4 dither matrix. Each effect is explained from first principles (model-view-projection pipeline, rasterization, perspective division) and then implemented in shader code. A practical checklist for historically accurate vs. aesthetically approximate PS1-style games is provided, along with a finished snowy scene built in Blender and Godot.

recent_posts.title: What is Perlin Noise?
recent_posts.summary: An explainer on Perlin noise, covering why white noise is unsuitable for organic-looking terrain and how Perlin noise solves this. Starts with pseudo-random number generation and hash functions on the GPU, then builds up value noise using linear interpolation on a lattice grid, smooth-step easing, and bilinear interpolation. Then explains gradient noise (Perlin noise) using dot products of random gradient vectors. Covers Ken Perlin's improvements: uniform gradient distribution on a sphere, predefined gradient sets, and switching from a 3rd-order to a 5th-order interpolant to fix second-derivative discontinuities that break analytical normal vector calculation. Briefly mentions simplex noise as a future topic.

recent_posts.title: The Problem With Procedural Generation
recent_posts.summary: A deep dive into the fundamental challenges of procedural generation in games, using the author's own fractal particle system project as a case study. The core problem: procedurally generated shapes escape the bounds of a voxel grid used for lighting. The solution involves GPU-based parallel reduction to compute an axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) of 4 million particles across multiple dispatches, then rescaling all particles to fit within the grid. The parallel reduction algorithm — a foundational GPU programming technique — reduces 4 million elements in ~0.6ms versus 9ms on CPU, demonstrating the power of GPU parallelism. The video also covers why procedural generation requires careful parameter constraints to avoid unplayable or unpleasant outcomes.
